Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "Making old things last longer"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english/ep-210624

Activity type: listening for the main idea and details about repair services in Sweden.
Language focus: verbs for maintenance and repair (fix, mend, repair, replace, throw away) and instructions.

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) Why does Sam say her day has been a nightmare? (gist)
2) How much rubbish does the world produce every year? (detail)
3) What does the company Fixi do, and how many orders did it take in its first six months? (detail)
4) What do Nudie Jeans promise their customers, and how much does a pair cost? (detail)
5) Researcher Jessika Richter talks about a peer effect. What does she hope will become mainstream again? (meaning)
6) What was the real inspiration for Fixi? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: She ripped her jeans, her computer stopped working and her car would not start.
- Q2: More than two billion tonnes.
- Q3: It collects broken bikes from your door and brings them back fixed. It took more than 600 orders.
- Q4: Free repairs for life. A pair costs about 150 dollars.
- Q5: Repairing broken things — a culture of repair and sustainable consumption.
- Q6: Rafi Mohammad was late for his lecture because of a flat tyre (answer c).

Phrase-capture instruction: write down every verb you hear for fixing things (fix, mend, repair) and for getting rid of things (throw away, replace). Then write two maintenance instructions with them, for example: "Repair the bike. Do not throw it away."

Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "Shocking facts about electricity"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english/ep-200514

Activity type: listening for technical facts about electrical systems in different countries.
Language focus: electrical terms (current, frequency, hertz, charge up) and safety rules with must and mustn't.

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) What do the letters AC and DC mean? (gist)
2) What does Georgina need when she travels to another country with her laptop? (detail)
3) What is the standard frequency in the US, and in the UK? (detail)
4) What does frequency mean for an electrical current? (vocabulary)
5) Why does Gareth's laptop still work in the United States? (detail)
6) Who is credited with discovering electricity, and what did he do? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: Alternating current and direct current — the two ways electricity flows.
- Q2: A converter plug.
- Q3: About 60 hertz in the US and about 50 hertz in the UK.
- Q4: The number of times an electrical wave repeats a positive-to-negative cycle. It is measured in hertz.
- Q5: Its power supply has solid-state electronics with a small converter, so it gives a DC supply and does not care about the AC frequency.
- Q6: Benjamin Franklin. He flew a kite with a metal key in a thunderstorm; the key conducted electricity and gave him a shock.

Phrase-capture instruction: Neil says that Franklin's experiment is not one he recommends trying at home. Write two safety rules for an electrical lab with must and mustn't, for example: "You mustn't touch a live conductor."

Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "Tech that refuses to die"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english_2024/ep-241017

Activity type: listening for examples and reasons why old technology is still used.
Language focus: time and frequency words (still, until recently, always, soon) and the idea of keeping equipment that still works.

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) Name two old technologies that Phil mentions at the start. (gist)
2) What does the word obsolete mean? (vocabulary)
3) What did the government of Japan use until recently, and what does CERN use to record its data? (detail)
4) What does the idiom "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" mean? (vocabulary)
5) Why did NASA engineer Jonathan Sauder design a clockwork rover for Venus? (detail)
6) Why does Dr Tacye Phillipson stick with the QWERTY keyboard? (detail)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: Any two: floppy disks, hand-held Game Boys, fax machines, Walkman cassette players.
- Q2: No longer in use because something newer or better has replaced it.
- Q3: Japan used 3.5-inch floppy disks for official documents; CERN uses magnetic tape reels.
- Q4: If something works well, there is no reason to change it.
- Q5: Ordinary electronics will not work on Venus: temperatures reach 460°C and the night is about 60 days long. The rover can be powered by Venus's winds.
- Q6: Everyone is used to it, and she does not want to learn the complicated keyboards that court reporters use.
- Quiz: the first home computer in the UK was the Sinclair ZX80 (1980).

Phrase-capture instruction: note the time and frequency words you hear (still, until recently, always, soon). Then write two sentences about equipment in your lab, for example: "We still use an old PLC because it always works."

Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "Is the recycling system broken?"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english/ep-200528

Activity type: listening for a process and the problems in it.
Language focus: the present simple passive for processes (waste is collected, is burned, is buried, is recycled).

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) Why was Neil late for the programme? (gist)
2) What happens to more and more household waste, according to Neil? (detail)
3) What did China stop doing in 2018? (detail)
4) What is virgin plastic? (vocabulary)
5) What did Professor Monic Sun's experiments show about recycling? (detail)
6) How much household waste did each person in the UK produce last year? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: He had forgotten to take the recycling bins out before the rubbish collection.
- Q2: It is incinerated (burned) or buried underground.
- Q3: It stopped accepting other countries' plastic and paper scrap. It used to take 55% of the world's scrap.
- Q4: New, unused plastic made directly from crude oil or natural gas.
- Q5: When people know that recycling is an option, they use more resources.
- Q6: 480 kg per person (answer b).

Phrase-capture instruction: listen for passive verbs (is incinerated, is buried, is recycled, is processed). Then describe in three passive sentences how waste is handled in your factory or city.

Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "The circular economy"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english/ep-200305

Activity type: listening for opinions and a definition.
Language focus: the modal passive (can be returned, can be reused, can be repaired) and words for products and responsibility.

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) What does Sam always do with her rubbish at home? (gist)
2) What is Neil's quiz question? (detail)
3) Why does Alexandre Lemille say that recycling is not the answer? (detail)
4) What does "out of sight, out of mind" mean? (vocabulary)
5) In a circular economy, what can always happen to a product such as a washing machine? (detail)
6) Which country recycles the highest percentage of its waste? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: She separates it into paper, metal, food, plastic and so on.
- Q2: Which country recycles the highest percentage of its waste: Sweden, Germany or New Zealand?
- Q3: We cannot separate all the waste properly, so it cannot be treated; a lot of waste is just hidden.
- Q4: We ignore or do not think about things that we cannot see.
- Q5: It can be returned to the manufacturer to be reused or repaired and then sold again. The manufacturer keeps responsibility for its lifecycle.
- Q6: Germany.

Phrase-capture instruction: write down the phrase "can always be returned to the manufacturer to be reused or repaired". Then write two sentences about machine parts with can be or must be + past participle.

items.titleEnglish: Should we wear a face mask?
items.contentMarkdown:
Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "Should we wear a face mask?"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english/ep-200702

Activity type: listening for evidence and opinions about protective equipment.
Language focus: purpose (to protect, to prevent) and risk language (a false sense of security).

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) Why have people in many countries started wearing face masks? (gist)
2) Rob mentions two times in history when people used masks. Name one. (detail)
3) What did Professor Robert West review, and what did he find? (detail)
4) What does the "stands to reason" argument say about masks? (detail)
5) How did the World Health Organisation's advice change in June? (detail)
6) Which two negative effects of masks does Professor West mention? (detail)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: To protect themselves and the people they come into contact with.
- Q2: The plagues of medieval Europe, or the 19th-century cholera outbreaks in the US.
- Q3: More than twenty studies. The evidence is equivocal — unclear.
- Q4: A covering in front of your face obviously traps a lot of the virus in the droplets you breathe or cough out.
- Q5: Masks should be worn in public where social distancing is not possible. Before, only people with symptoms and their carers had to wear them.
- Q6: Mask shaming and a false sense of security.
- Quiz: masks were first widely used in 1905 in Chicago (answer b), when Dr Alice Hamilton noticed that carers who wore masks did not get sick.

Phrase-capture instruction: write down the purpose phrases you hear (to protect, to prevent). Then explain the purpose of two PPE items in your workshop, for example: "We wear safety glasses to protect our eyes from metal chips."

Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "Can you stop a disaster?"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english_2023/ep-230803

Activity type: listening for examples of emergency planning and warning systems.
Language focus: emergency language (warning, shelter, evacuation, evacuation routes) and a review of this week's grammar.

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) What is unusual about the park ranger Roy Sullivan? (gist)
2) About how many people died in natural disasters around the world in the last decade? (detail)
3) Why does Professor Lucy Easthope think we should not call disasters natural? (detail)
4) Give one example of additional harm after a disaster. (detail)
5) How are people in Bangladesh warned that a cyclone is coming? (detail)
6) Which natural disaster causes the most human deaths now? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: He was struck by lightning seven times and survived every time.
- Q2: About half a million people.
- Q3: The word suggests fatalism — that nothing can be done — but a lot of the harm can be prevented.
- Q4: The spread of disease, or destroyed roads and buildings.
- Q5: People on bicycles use megaphones to tell everyone to go to a shelter. People know the evacuation routes. Cyclone deaths fell a hundredfold.
- Q6: Earthquakes (answer a).

Phrase-capture instruction: note the emergency words you hear (warning, shelter, evacuation, evacuation routes). Then write three instructions for an evacuation from your workshop, for example: "When the alarm sounds, leave by the nearest emergency exit."
